meta_description: Identity modernization measured at revocation: HR-event-driven lifecycle, rotation on SLA across every identity class, stale credentials at or below 2% and auditors satisfied first.

blocks.x: Identity lifecycle done properly: joiner-mover-leaver automation that revokes on the leaver SLA, privileged access in vaults instead of spreadsheets, standing admin accounts driven to zero — and MFA that people actually complete.
Identity is the perimeter now — and it runs on process
blocks.sub: Lifecycle fidelity, brokered privilege and workload identity as the program

blocks.x: Identity is where most breaches begin and where most programs under-invest: accounts outlive their owners, service accounts share passwords, and privileged access is granted with a ticket and forgotten. Modernization is lifecycle engineering — every identity born with an owner, moved with re-attestation, and killed on schedule.

Machine identity gets the same discipline as humans: workload identities with short-lived credentials, secrets vaulted and rotated, and the hygiene score reported weekly because credential rot is a countdown, not an event.
Below: the failure modes that turn identity programs into audit findings, the reference architecture of the lifecycle, and the console that keeps revocation honest.

Revocation is the metric that matters
blocks.sub: Lifecycle fidelity, brokered privilege and workload identity — where auditors look first

blocks.x: Identity programs are judged on the unglamorous metric: how fast access disappears when it should. The lifecycle runs HR-driven — joiner, mover and leaver events drive provisioning with SLAs, and the leaver path is verified, not assumed: revocation is confirmed across every downstream estate (IdP, SaaS, VPN, legacy LDAP), with the confirmation logged per system. Privileged access is brokered, not owned: standing admin grants are eliminated in favor of just-in-time elevation from a vault, with session recording on every privileged minute.

Workload identity is the modern frontier — service principals with static secrets are the new service accounts nobody rotated; the modernization replaces them with short-lived, SPIFFE-class workload identities where the platform supports it, and hygiene scoring keeps the honest count everywhere else. The console reads revocation SLA adherence, MFA coverage and hygiene scores; auditors read the same numbers, which is the point.

items: Revocation confirmed per downstream system, logged — never assumed.

Why is revocation the metric that matters?

Because auditors find leavers first: an ex-contractor with live credentials invalidates every access review on paper. Revocation SLA is measured from the HR event to verified revocation across every downstream estate — the console headline is exactly that number.
What makes HR the source of truth?

The lifecycle starts at the HR event: joiner, mover and leaver events drive provisioning, transfer and revocation. Downstream estates reconcile to HR truth, and drift between them is a gate metric, not a discovered surprise.
How are service and workload identities handled?

As first-class identity classes: rotation on SLA (95–96%), ownership named, standing privilege minimized. Break-glass accounts run at 100% rotation with every use alarmed — the chart shows each class honestly.
Can you modernize without a rip-and-replace of our IAM?
Yes — the lifecycle plane overlays the existing IAM: HR truth feeds it, revocation verification runs across what exists, and the defaults table names where an identity store earns a deviation.
What does the IAM team inherit?
The lifecycle plane, the console with revocation and rotation metrics, the gates and the privileged-access overlay — the team operates on SLAs, not on tickets nobody closes.

blocks.x: Ask how fast your last leaver actually lost access — then ask who verified it. The diagnostic will measure your real revocation SLA and vault your privilege before your auditor asks.
